West Side Story. The nineteen fifty-seven musical by Leonard Bernstein, music, Stephen Sondheim, lyrics, and Arthur Laurents, book, that transplants Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet to nineteen fifty's New York City, replacing feuding families with rival street gangs—the Jets, who are white, and the Sharks, who are Puerto Rican—exploring themes of prejudice, youth, and violence in an urban American setting.

This landmark collaboration between Bernstein and the young Sondheim elevated musical-theatre music to symphonic complexity. It contains some of the most famous musical-theatre songs: "Somewhere," "America," "Tonight," "Officer Krupke," and the instrumental "Rumble." The Rumble scene replaces a sword fight with a choreographed gang battle set to orchestral music, a fusion of dance, drama, and symphonic underscoring.

The show opens with a brief overture and uses Bernstein's jazz and Latin influences to capture nineteen fifty's urban America. The score won the Tony Award and was adapted into an Academy Award-winning film released in nineteen sixty-one. The plot follows Tony, an ex-Jet, and Maria, a Shark's sister, who fall in love despite gang loyalty, leading to tragedy and social commentary rather than romantic resolution.

The show was directed and choreographed by Jerome Robbins, whose innovative dance vocabulary became inseparable from the show's identity. It won ten Tony Awards in nineteen fifty-eight. The nineteen sixty-one film won ten Academy Awards, making it one of the most decorated theatrical works in American history.
